newsitem.title: VENEZUELA: LatAm stocks seen jarred in volatile week.
newsitem.headline: LatAm stocks seen jarred in volatile week.

text.p: Latin American stocks are seen volatile in a bumpy week as U.S. drug certification makes waves in Mexico, while expected early gains in Brazil and Argentina on a rising Wall Street are expected to be pared later by factors at home.

Chilean stocks are seen lackluster as hopes of interest cuts fade. And the Venezuelan bolsa is still shaky after last week's heady cocktail of coup rumors, delayed telephone rate increases and brawling politicians dropped the leading .IBC index over seven percent to Friday's 6,237.29 close, traders and analysts said.
"We have been surprised by the extent to which rumors of potential coups and political unrest have upended Venezuela's IBC," said New York-based IDEA in a market commentary.
While the drop could represent a buying opportunity, IDEA added, the market will be watching for a clear decision on telephone company CANTV's stalled second quarter 4.18 percent rate increase.
Brazilian shares are seen riding continuing optimism fed by expected rises on Wall Street and the upcoming privatization of state mining giant CVRD.

But Brazilian trade deficit data due Tuesday, and an expected Supreme Court ruling on the legality of selling Band B telecommunication concessions may dent investor confidence, which helped firm the index 3.9 percent to 9,181 points last week, traders said.
In Argentina, stocks are seen tied to Wall Street for lack of local data, with the MerVal index rising early in the week to a top of 745-750 points, but later switching to losses.
"The trend is very undecided, but we should follow through on Friday's gains for a day or two," said Interfin broker Jorge Bonanno.
Buenos Aires' blue-chip index bounced Friday to end the week up 1.8 percent at 730.36 when U.S. February employment figures suggested non-inflationary U.S. growth.
Chilean shares are expected to angle lower after rumors late last week of a cut in interest rates failed to materialize -- but lack of local data should see trade rangebound.

"Stock prices will adjust downwards, but then the market should be stable," said Guillermo Tagel, head of research at Santander Investments. The 40-share .IPSA index ended up 0.84 percent on the week Friday at 116.94 points.
In Mexico, weak trade is seen keeping the .MXX index tightly bound as the U.S. Congress ponders Mexican certification as a drug war ally.

On Friday, U.S. President Bill Clinton said he was convinced his certification of Mexico's effort in the war against drugs was correct. But while opposing Congressional efforts to reverse his decision, Clinton has yet to say whether he would veto any joint Congressional resolution to decertify.
